body.text: The SG4 Group, a company comprising the four Malaysian states ruled by the Parti Islam SeMalaysia (PAS), recently hosted a high-level Business and Economic Forum. Themed “Four States, One Economic Vision”, the hall in the Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre was at full capacity, attended by government representatives, economists, industry leaders and diplomats. SG4 has ambitious plans to agglomerate economic state power by leveraging collective resources to accelerate economic growth and development. This goal is laudable, but the states still face uphill challenges and structural realities in achieving these goals.

PAS, which is the largest federal opposition party in Malaysia, governs Kedah, Kelantan and Terengganu on its own, and is in a coalition with the Malay party Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu) in Perlis. Formed two years ago to consolidate bargaining power, the SG4 Group seeks to pool the four rural states’ resources to share wealth equitably. The quartet of states has a collective population of 5.7 million people spread over a land mass of 38,000 square kilometres. In prepared remarks read out on his behalf, SG4 advisor Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamed speech called the four states “a sleeping giant”. With land, resources and people as the main assets, he stated that the states are blessed with rare earth elements (REE), which are used in applications such as clean energy applications, consumer electronics and military hardware such as precision-guided missiles and radar. These REE sources can potentially provide SG4 with a substantial source of income. Seventy per cent of Malaysia’s REE inferred reserves reportedly lie within the four states’ perimeters.

Indeed, each state showcased their respective current industrial practices and future potential, ranging from the petrochemicals, manufacturing and semiconductor industries to agro-industry, tourism and logistics. SG4’s pitch is to connect industrial development with green energy, logistics and workforce preparation across all four states. A major gap, however, would be SG4’s ability to attract the right talent and skilled labour required for an ambitious industrial development plan.

SG4’s economic vision is clear. In his opening address, Terengganu Chief Minister Dr Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar cited 2019 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences winner Abhijit Banerjee, who noted that stable employment, healthcare access, education quality and wealth distribution are the true markers of public welfare — not merely GDP numbers alone. A PAS-led government would, according to him, cater to different, economic, geographical, culture and religious beliefs. Whether this form of governance comes to fruition will still need to be tested.

The main challenge for SG4 will be competition and conflict between the federal government and the four states. SG4 wants autonomy over lucrative resources and more independent economic policymaking. However, constitutional, fiscal and regulatory control resides in Putrajaya.
SG4’s forum and proposals could lay the groundwork for more decentralised federalism in Malaysia, which Putrajaya could consider incorporating immediately.

The REE sector is a perfect case study. The states control land, natural resources and exploratory mining licenses for REE extraction, but Putrajaya controls export and import licenses, environmental regulation and national industrial roadmaps. The federal government recently relaxed its ban on exporting raw REE abroad under new guidelines, by permitting exports of up to 100 metric tonnes for research and development, or by agreeing to set up a processing facility in Malaysia within three years. Yet the states were not consulted on this prior to its announcement (according to the author’s interview with Terengganu Strategic and Integrity Institute, 28 October 2026). Such policy bottlenecks could stalemate what could potentially be the largest revenue source for SG4.

Dr Ahmad Samsuri also suggested a “major framework”, such as a federal-state fiscal and development equalisation formula. One example of this is to enable a portion of taxes generated by states, but collected by Putrajaya, to be returned to the respective states. The federal government collects almost all income, corporate and sales taxes, leaving states with only land tax, forestry, water and tourism tax revenues. Since state borrowing requires federal government approval, SG4 would not be able to self-finance large-scale infrastructure or green energy grids.

If stronger state economies can contribute to a stronger Malaysia, as he argues, then the key to strengthening states is to “develop more productive activities and contribute to more national growth”. States would have the freedom to decide what infrastructure development projects they undertake, as opposed to being subject to the federal government’s political calculations. Each of the SG4 states owns 25 per cent of the company; thus, revenues from REEs, which are more present in Terengganu and Kelantan, are to be distributed equally across all four states. This could strengthen state capacity and balance unequal regional development.

Finally, Dr Ahmad Samsuri said that “cooperation between federal and state government” was essential, and should PAS become part of the federal government after the 16th General Election (GE16), such cooperation would be strengthened within the federation. Indeed, the 1956 Reid Commission that drafted Malaya’s independence constitution stated that close co-operation between the States and the Federation would “promote the interests of all concerned and be of great benefit to the nation”. Unfortunately, the Commission stopped short of specifying such co-operation in the Constitution. SG4 might strengthen its economic position in the future through the Marang Terminal. The private facility in Terengganu was built to ship out processed silica, and helps to strengthen state royalties and government-linked company (GLC) equity revenue streams. While SG4’s strategy may ultimately be premised on taking Putrajaya, a more institutionalised and permanent mechanism would be a more ideal long-term solution.

SG4’s proposals could lay the groundwork for more decentralised federalism in Malaysia, which Putrajaya could consider incorporating immediately. Until GE16 happens, Putrajaya and SG4 could begin to pioneer a formal framework for resource revenue-sharing and decentralised economic policymaking beyond the platforms currently available. This is especially true since there is no certainty that any one coalition will win. Unless this takes place, the “sleeping giant” will remain in slumber, constrained by Malaysia’s highly centralised federation. But if — as PAS has hinted strongly in the forum — they take control of Putrajaya and retain SG4 states, development of the currently relatively rural states may have a higher chance of success.
